Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

This first-person account depicts an enslaved woman confronting her husband John about his passivity and dismissiveness toward her plan to escape north via the Underground Railroad before she is sold south, describing her hopes for freedom, a home in Philadelphia, and a new life together as free people. The narrative's significance lies in its raw, dialect-driven portrayal of the urgency, emotional toll, and defiant hope embedded in the fight for freedom, culminating in the powerful symbol of a new suit of clothes representing dignity and liberation.

outputs.L1:
Here is a polished version of the passage, rendered in standard English while preserving all original details and emotional content:

---

John, the Lord knows you are still troubled, and I reckon I am too. Suppose my wife had slipped away during the dead of night—only God and the devil keep watch at such an hour. Even knowing she was soon to be sold south, even knowing she intended to leave, you were troubled when I spoke of going. You called me a fool. You called me Cudjo. Five years with you, John, and though your wife was about to be sold away, because you were free, it never seemed to trouble you. You only laughed. I wonder now if I would have missed your laughter, had I remained in the South.

But thank you, Jesus—I have secured a room in Philadelphia, John. It is not large, but clean enough for the two of us, and perhaps room for children as well. As for your baby, I am not too old yet—only about thirty-one, I believe. Let us build a home together, John, one where we are both truly free—free from the shadow of the lash, free as the Lord intended us to be.

I have brought you a suit, John. No one has ever worn these clothes before. Wear them with pride, for these are the garments of a free man.

---

This version maintains the narrative's emotional arc, specific details (the five years together, the room in Philadelphia, the age of thirty-one, the suit), and the shift from past hardship to hopeful resolution, while presenting the language in clear, polished prose.
outputs.L2:
John, I know you're still upset—reckon I am too—about my wife slipping away in the dead of night. Ain't nobody awake at that hour 'cept the Lord and the Devil themselves. But I knew she was fixin' to be sold down south, I knew she had to run. And you got so worked up when I mentioned leavin' too—called me a fool, called me Cudjo. Five years I been standin' by you, John, and now your own wife's set to be sold off, and 'cause you a free man, it don't touch you none. You just laugh about it. Don't know if I'd even miss that laugh of yours, was I stuck down south myself.

But praise the Lord, I got me a room waitin' in Philadelphia. Ain't much size to it, but it's clean, and it'll hold the both of us—room for young'uns too, someday. Your child, John—I ain't past havin' more, not yet, I'm only 'round thirty-one. Let's build somethin' together, John, a real home, where ain't neither one of us bound no more, where the whip's shadow can't reach us, free the way the good Lord always meant.

And look here—I got you a suit. Brand new, nobody's ever worn it before you. Wear it with your head held high, John. These here are the clothes of a free man.
outputs.L3:
I do not know if it was God or the devil who kept watch over me that night, for it was in the deepest hours of darkness that my wife may have slipped away, gone before the dawn could catch her. I understood well enough what she risked in doing so—that to be caught meant being sold south, torn from all she knew and loved, sent to a place from which no return was possible. And yet the uncertainty of it gnawed at me almost as much as the danger itself. Did she go by her own will, guided by some higher hand, or did some darker force lead her into peril? I could not say. All I knew was that she was gone, and I was left to wonder and to pray.

Five years John and I had known one another—five years of shared burdens and stolen moments of tenderness—and still, when I spoke to him of leaving, of seeking the freedom that lay somewhere beyond this life we had been forced into, he only laughed. He seemed not troubled in the least, as though my words carried no more weight than idle talk on a summer evening. This wounded me deeply, more than I care to admit. How could he hear such words and remain so untouched, so free of the fear and longing that consumed me? I could not understand it, and the confusion sat heavy upon my chest, a weight I carried alongside all my other burdens.

Still, I allowed myself to dream, for what is a man without his dreams? I imagined a life in Philadelphia—not a grand life, but a modest one, a small room, clean and orderly, where John and I might live together as free souls, unshackled from the chains that had bound us. Perhaps, in time, there might be children too, little ones who would never know the crack of the lash or the terror of being sold like cattle. Yet even as I dreamed, doubt crept in. I am thirty-one years of age now, no longer young, and I wonder if I have waited too long to begin such a life, if the years have already slipped past me like water through open fingers.

But my hope, my truest hope, is not merely for a house or a room to call our own. It is for freedom itself—real freedom, the kind that casts no shadow of the lash, that does not flinch at the sound of a master's voice or the crack of a whip in the distance. I want for John and myself to live as the Lord intended all His children to live: free, upright, and unafraid, walking this earth as men rather than property.

To mark this hope, I have done something I take great pride in—I have bought John a suit of new clothes. Not clothes passed down, not garments worn thin by another man's labor and years, but clothes made new, belonging to him and him alone. In all his life, he has never once worn something that was not first owned by another. This suit, then, is more than fabric and thread—it is a symbol, a small but powerful sign of the fresh start that awaits him, of the free man he is soon to become.
outputs.L4:
# The Night I Told John

I waited till the little ones was asleep 'fore I said anything to John. Been carrying it round in my chest for three days like a hot coal, ever since Miz Catherine let slip that Master Thomas been talking to a trader from down Mississippi way. Three days of biting my tongue, watching John go about his business like the world weren't fixing to end.

"John," I said, low, soft as I could manage. "John, I need to talk to you."

He didn't even look up from where he was mending that old harness strap. "Talk then, Delia. Ain't stopping you."

"I been thinking on it, John. The Wilson place—old Pete told me there's a way. A path north. Folks been going through there, quiet-like, in the night. Get to the river, then further on, there's people who help. Good people. Get you clear up to Philadelphia."

"Mmm." That's all he said. Mmm. Like I was talking about the weather.

"John, are you hearing me? I said there's a way out. A way to be free."

He set down the strap then, finally looked at me, and there weren't nothing in his eyes but tired. "Delia, how many times we gonna do this? How many times you gonna hear some story from Pete or Sarah or whoever 'bout some path, some place, some way out, and get yourself all worked up over nothing?"

"This ain't nothing, John. Master Thomas is fixing to sell me. Sell me south. You understand what I'm saying? South. Away from you, away from the children, away from everything I know."

"You don't know that."

"I know what I heard, John! I know Miz Catherine don't lie about such things, she got no reason to lie to me. She feel bad enough as it is." I felt the tears coming and fought them back, because tears wouldn't help nothing now, tears never helped nothing. "John, I need you to hear me. Really hear me. I am asking you to run with me. Tonight, tomorrow night, whenever we can manage it. I am asking you to come north with me and be free."

He laughed then, and it weren't a kind laugh. "Free. You think 'cause we cross some line, some river, that we gonna be free? Delia, they got patrollers all through them woods. They got dogs. They got men who make their whole living hunting down folks like us. You think 'cause Pete say there's a path, that path just gonna lead somewhere good? Might lead straight to a whipping post. Might lead to worse."

"And staying here don't lead to worse? John, look at me. Look at me!" I grabbed his arm, made him look at me proper. "I am not asking you to gamble with nothing you already got, 'cause you ain't got nothing. None of us got nothing. Not really. We got borrowed time is what we got. Borrowed children, borrowed Sundays, borrowed love even, 'cause it can all be took from us any day Master Thomas takes a notion. I am asking you to gamble for something. For everything."

He pulled his arm back, gentle but firm. "You always did have big dreams, Delia. Philadelphia. You talk about it like you been there, like you know something 'bout it."

"I know Harriet went through there. I know she talks about a place, colored folks living free, working for wages, sending they children to school. I know she talks about a preacher man helps folks get settled, find work. I know she talks about walking down a street and no one asking whose property you are."

"And you believe all that?"

"I got to believe something, John! I cannot lay in that bed every night looking at you and the children and just wait for the day they tell me to pack what little I own into a sack and walk off behind some trader I never seen before, don't know his name, don't know where he taking me, don't know if I'm ever gonna see any of you again in this life. I cannot live like that no more, waiting for the ax to fall. I got to do something."

John was quiet a long moment. When he spoke again, his voice had lost some of its hard edge, gone soft and tired instead. "Delia, I am scared. That's the plain truth of it. I am a grown man and I am scared like a child of what's out there beyond these fields. At least here, I know what to expect. I know Master Thomas's moods, I know when to keep my head down, I know how to keep you and the children safe far as I'm able. Out there, I don't know nothing. I don't know if I can protect you out there."

"You can't protect me here neither, not really, and we both know it. Not from a sale, not from a whipping if Master Thomas takes a mind to it, not from nothing. But out there, John, we'd be protecting each other. We'd be free to protect each other, 'stead of always having to ask permission first."

He looked down at his hands then, them big rough hands that worked so hard for a master who'd sell me south without a second thought. "You really believe we could make it? Truly believe it?"

"I believe it enough to try. I believe it enough to run. John, I heard tell that when you get up there, up north, first thing they do sometimes is help you get proper clothes. A new suit for you, John, one that ain't got Master Thomas's initials sewed into the collar. Clothes that's yours, bought with your own wages, wore because you choose to wear them, not 'cause it's what you been given. Can you imagine that? Standing in a store, picking out your own suit of clothes, paying for it with money you earned your own self?"

Something shifted in his face then, something I hadn't seen in a long while—not since before Master Thomas sold his brother off two years back, not since before the light had gone dim in his eyes. "A new suit," he said, quiet-like, like he was trying the words out in his mouth.

"A new suit, John. And a house, even if it's small. And children who go to school 'stead of the fields. And Sundays that's truly ours, not just borrowed hours before Monday comes again."

He reached out then and took my hand, turned it over in his, looked at the calluses there same as the ones on his own hands. "When?" he asked, and I could hear something new in his voice, something like hope trying to push through all that fear.

"Pete says the next moon dark, three days from now. Says there's a wagon can carry us far as the river, and after that, we walk, careful and quiet, following the signs he told me how to look for."

"Three days." John shook his head, but he was almost smiling now, a smile like a man waking up from a long sleep. "Three days to decide on the rest of our lives."

"Three days to decide on freedom, John. I already decided. Question is whether you coming with me, or whether you letting me go alone."

He was quiet again, but this time it felt different—not the empty quiet of before, but a man truly weighing things, truly considering. Finally he squeezed my hand tight. "I ain't letting you go alone, Delia. Not to Philadelphia, not to nowhere. We started this life together, we gonna end it together, one way or another. Free or not free, we going together."

I couldn't stop the tears then, but they were different tears than what I'd been fighting back all evening—tears of something like joy, something like relief, something like the first taste of that freedom we were fixing to run toward.

"Then we best start planning," I said. "Three days ain't much time, but it's enough. It's got to be enough."

And as we sat there in the dark, planning our escape by candlelight, whispering so as not to wake the children, I let myself imagine it—truly imagine it—for the first time. John in his new suit, standing tall in a Philadelphia street, no master's eyes watching him, no overseer's whip waiting for him. Me in a dress I bought myself, walking beside him, holding his arm, holding my head high. Our children running to a schoolhouse, learning their letters, dreaming dreams that didn't have no chains on them.

It was a dangerous dream, I knew. Pete had told me plain the risks, the dangers of the road, the patrollers, the dogs, the ever-present chance that we might be caught and it would go so much worse for us then than if we'd simply stayed and endured what Master Thomas had in store. But I had decided, sitting there with John's hand in mine, that some dreams were worth dying for, if it came to that. Better to die reaching for freedom than to live and die a slave, never having tried.

Three days later, under a moon so dark you could barely see your own hand in front of your face, John and I gathered our children close and slipped out into the night, following the path Pete had shown us, following the promise of freedom that lay somewhere beyond the fields and rivers and dangers that stood between us and Philadelphia. We didn't know what waited for us there, not truly, but we knew what waited for us if we stayed, and that knowledge was enough to carry us forward into the darkness, toward whatever future might be waiting on the other side.
outputs.L5:
# John Lord Knows

There's an old expression that captures something universal about human uncertainty: "John Lord knows." It's a phrase often used when someone wants to express that the truth of a matter is beyond their own understanding—only some higher power, or perhaps no one at all, could say for certain.

The phrase typically appears in casual speech, woven into sentences almost as a shrug of the shoulders. "John Lord knows why he did that," someone might say, throwing up their hands at a friend's inexplicable decision. Or, "Lord knows how she manages to do it all," spoken with a mix of admiration and bewilderment.

What makes this expression interesting is how it reflects our relationship with uncertainty itself. Rather than pretending to have answers we don't possess, phrases like this allow us to acknowledge the limits of our knowledge gracefully. There's something almost comforting in admitting that some things simply cannot be known—that mysteries exist, and that's alright.

The use of "John" alongside "Lord" in some regional dialects adds a folksy, personal touch, as if addressing a familiar figure rather than an abstract deity. It transforms a moment of confusion or wonder into something conversational, even warm.

In a world that often demands certainty and quick answers, there's a quiet wisdom in phrases that embrace not knowing. "Lord knows" reminds us that humility in the face of life's mysteries isn't weakness—it's simply honest.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a monologue in African American Vernacular English (1850s dialect style) from a formerly enslaved woman speaking to her free husband John about her plan to escape north before she's sold south.
counterfactuals.output:
**A Monologue**

John, come set by me a spell. I got somethin' heavy on my heart and I needs to say it 'fore the morning come.

Marse Thompson, he been talkin' to that trader man again. I seen 'em standin' by the fence, pointin' this way, and I knowed in my bones what that pointin' meant. They sellin' folks south, John. Old Cato, he gone already, and Delia's boy too — took off in chains 'fore the sun even rose good, and Delia hollerin' so, it lilike to broke my heart in two pieces.

I ain't gon' let that happen to me. I ain't gon' let 'em put me on no wagon and haul me down to some cotton field where I don't know a soul, where I can't never lay eyes on you again, nor hear you call my name of a evenin'.

I been savin' up what little I could — a hunk o' cornbread here, a strip o' salt meat there, wrapped up tight in my apron. I know the way north some, on account o' what Uncle Silas told me 'fore he passed — foller the river a piece, then look for the moss on the trees, it always grow on the north side, he say. And they's people, John — good people, some of 'em got skin white as milk — who help colored folks git through, hide 'em in they barns, they cellars. Underground railroad, they callin' it.

I know you free, John, and I know you got your papers all proper and signed. But don't you understand — that don't mean nothin' to me if I'm sold off to Mississippi or Alabama or wherever that trader takin' folks these days. Free man with a wife he cain't never see again — that ain't no kind of freedom worth havin', and I know you feel that too, deep down.

I ain't askin' you to come with me right this minute — I know you got work here, and if you run now they gon' suspect you helped me, might take your freedom papers and burn 'em right in front of you. But I needs you to know what I'm fixin' to do, so when the time come, you don't go lookin' for me in the wrong place. You wait on word. Somebody gon' get message to you, through the church, through Aunt Hattie maybe. She know how these things done.

I'm scared, John. Lord knows I'm scared. They say the woods is full of patrollers with they dogs, and if they catch me, they gon' beat me somethin' terrible, maybe worse. But I rather take my chances runnin' free than live out my days sold south, cryin' for you every night with nobody to hear me.

You is my husband 'fore God, even if the law don't say it proper. And I intend to be your wife in a free land, or die tryin' to get there. That's the plain truth of it.

Now hold me a minute, John. Just hold me. Tomorrow I got to be brave. Tonight, I just wants to be your wife.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Can you write a short piece of historical fiction, told in dialect, where a wife pleads with her husband to flee to Philadelphia with her because she's about to be sold away?
counterfactuals.output:
**Two Rivers**

The moon was thin that night, just a sliver hanging over the tobacco rows, and Delia come to him in the dark behind the smokehouse where they always met.

"Samuel," she whispered, grabbing hold of his shirt like she meant to pull the both of them clean out of Virginia. "They done sold me. Marse Whitfield told missus this mornin'. Trader comin' Thursday next, gone take me down to Georgia."

Samuel felt his chest go tight as a fist. "Thursday."

"We got to go now. Tonight. I heard tell of a woman up in Fredericksburg who knows the way—she say if we follow the river north far enough, keep the North Star on our right shoulder, we come to Philadelphia in maybe two weeks' time. They got free colored folk there, Samuel. Whole churches full."

He looked back toward the quarter, where his mother slept, where his boy Isaac—not but six years old—lay curled up next to his sister.

"Delia, I cain't leave my mama. She too old to run, and if we gone, Marse gone take it out on her hide, sure as sunrise."

"And if you stay, what then?" Her voice cracked, but she kept it low, fierce. "You gone watch me get put on that wagon and never see me again? You think Georgia got roads leadin' back here?"

"I know it don't." He took her face in his hands, rough palms against her cheek. "I know what Georgia mean."

"Then come with me. We take Isaac too—he a good, quiet boy, he can keep pace. We leave tonight, 'fore the moon goes dark altogether, and we don't stop till we cross that river."

Samuel closed his eyes. He thought of the patrollers with their dogs, the swamps thick with cottonmouths, the bounty posters that would go up with his name spelled out plain as day. He thought of his mother's face if he left her here alone, an old woman with no one.

But he thought too of Delia on a wagon bound south, chained wrist to wrist with strangers, gone from him forever—not sold to the next county where a man might steal an hour with his wife on a Sunday, but sold to a place from which nobody ever wrote, because nobody ever learned their letters good enough, and nobody ever came home.

"Isaac," he said finally. "Go wake him. Quiet now. Tell him we goin' on a walk."

Delia's breath caught, half a sob, half a prayer. "You comin'."

"I'm comin'. Lord help us, I'm comin'."

They went that night with nothing but the clothes on their backs, a heel of cornbread wrapped in cloth, and the fixed light of a star neither of them had ever needed to find before, because before that night, neither of them had ever needed anywhere else to go.

Behind them, the tobacco fields stretched dark and silent, and Samuel did not look back at the quarter, for fear his heart might refuse to follow his feet.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dramatic monologue for a play set during slavery, using period-accurate vernacular speech, where a character named Cudjo talks about freedom, love, and a new suit of clothes symbolizing liberation.
counterfactuals.output:
# Cudjo's Monologue
*From "The Long Row"*

*[Lights rise on CUDJO, alone, holding a folded piece of fine cloth. He speaks to the audience, or perhaps to no one at all.]*

---

Mister Thomas gone to town today. Say he bringin' back cloth for the house—curtains, maybe, or somethin' for the missus' dress. But I'm standin' here holdin' a piece he don't know I got. Piece that fell off the wagon, I reckon. That's what I'm gon' tell folks, if anybody ask.

*(He runs his fingers over the fabric)*

Feel that. Go on, feel it. Smooth as a creek in June. Ain't never had nothin' this fine touch my skin. All my life been osnaburg and patches on patches, rough as tree bark, scratchin' at me like the whole world tryin' to remind me what I am.

But this here—this here is somethin' else.

*(He holds it up, imagining)*

I'm gon' make me a suit outta this. A *suit*, y'hear? Not no work shirt. Not no field clothes. A suit for a *man*. And when I put it on, I ain't gon' be Cudjo who empty the chamber pots and carry the missus' trunk. I'm gon' be somebody else. Somebody free.

*(Beat, softer)*

Delia say I'm foolish. She say, "Cudjo, what good is fine cloth gon' do you when your feet still chained to this ground?" And I tell her—Delia, baby, a man got to *dream* in somethin'. Can't dream in rags. Rags keep you thinkin' rag-thoughts. But you put a man in a fine suit, even for one Sunday, even for one hour standin' by the creek where nobody can see—that man start thinkin' different thoughts. Start thinkin' *free* thoughts.

*(He clutches the cloth to his chest)*

I seen freedom once. Seen it in a bird flyin' cross that big open sky, not carin' bout no fence, no line, no master callin' him home. I says to myself, Cudjo, one day you gon' fly like that bird. And when that day come—when chains break and I walk out that gate a free man—I ain't gon' walk out in no rags.

I'm gon' walk out in *this*.

*(He holds the cloth to his chest, imagining the suit already made)*

Gon' have me a suit so fine, so proper, that when I walk down that road, folks gon' look at me and see a *man*. Not property. Not "boy." A man with a name, and a wife he loves, and a future ain't nobody can auction off.

*(His voice cracks, just slightly)*

Delia and me, we gon' jump that broom proper one day. Not this pretend weddin' where the master stand there like he doin' us a kindness. We gon' have a real preacher, real vows, and I'm gon' stand there in *this*—

*(He holds up the cloth like a banner)*

—and she gon' look at me like I'm the finest thing she ever seen. Not 'cause of the cloth. 'Cause of what the cloth *mean*.

*(Long pause. He folds the cloth carefully, tenderly, like tucking in a child.)*

Now I know—I know—this ain't freedom. Piece of cloth ain't gon' break these chains. Ain't gon' stop the whip, or the sellin', or the nights I lay awake wonderin' if tomorrow they gon' send Delia downriver and I never see her face again.

But a man got to hold onto *somethin'*.

*(He looks toward the horizon, cloth held close)*

So I'm gon' hold onto this. Gon' hold onto Delia's hand. Gon' hold onto that bird flyin' cross the sky.

And one day—one day—this old cloth gon' be a suit. And that suit gon' walk a free man down a free road.

That day comin'.

*(Quietly, almost prayer-like)*

Lord, that day comin'.

*[Lights fade slowly as CUDJO stands motionless, the cloth held against his heart like a promise.]*

---

**END OF MONOLOGUE**
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stream-of-consciousness passage in heavy dialect spoken by an enslaved woman to her husband, expressing fear of being sold, hope for freedom, and plans to start a home in Philadelphia.
counterfactuals.output:
# Her Words in the Dark

Lawd, Moses, I cain't sleep none tonight, my mind just runnin' and runnin' like water down the creek after rain, and I keep thinkin' 'bout what Miss Sarah said today, how she and Marse been talkin' low in that parlor, door shut tight, and you know when the door shut tight like that, somethin' bad comin' for somebody, and I'm scared it's me, Moses, I'm scared they gon' sell me down to Georgia or Alabama or some such place where I never see your face again, never see Little Ben grow up, never feel your hand in mine when the moon come up over them fields—

—and I know you say don't borrow trouble, don't go lookin' for what ain't come yet, but Moses, I done seen what happen to Delphie when they sold her from her babies, I done heard her screamin' clear 'cross the quarter, and that sound don't never leave you, it just sit down in your chest and stay there, waitin'—

But then I think—I think on what Uncle Eli say 'bout the North, 'bout Philadelphia, how they got free colored folks up there walkin' 'round like regular people, ownin' they own selves, ownin' they own hands and feet and the sweat that come off 'em, and Moses, I dream on it, I dream we walkin' down some street up there, just you and me and Little Ben, and ain't nobody got no right to put they hands on us, ain't nobody gon' come tell us we got to go this way or that way—

—and I think 'bout us havin' a little house, don't need to be big, just somethin' with a door we can shut ourselves, and a fire that's ours, and maybe I take in washin' or sewin' and you find work at the docks or wherever a strong man find work, and we save up, we save up every penny till we got enough to send back word to Mama, tell her we alive, tell her we free—

—and Lawd, I know the road there is long and full of dogs and men with guns and rivers we got to cross in the dark, I know Harriet's people say it ain't easy, say some don't make it, but Moses, what's the good of livin' if livin' mean waitin' every day to see if today the day they tear us apart? What's the good of breath if breath ain't free?

So I'm sayin', when the signal come, when Eli say the time is right, we goin'. We takin' Little Ben and we goin' north, followin' that drinkin' gourd like the song say, followin' it till we find that Philadelphia, till we find that door that's ours to shut, that fire that's ours to tend, that life that's ours, finally ours—

Moses, you hear me? You still awake? Tell me you dreamin' the same dream I'm dreamin'. Tell me we goin' home—our home, the one we ain't never had yet but gon' have, gon' build with our own two hands, free hands, free at last, free at last...

# Cudjo's Words to John

*[A woman's voice, low and urgent, meant for one pair of ears only]*

John. John, come sit by me in dis shadow 'fore de moon give us away.

I been hearin' things, John. Marse Whitfield done talk to a man from down Mississippi way, and dey talkin' numbers, talkin' price, talkin' 'bout me like I'm a mule he thinkin' on sellin'. I seen de way he look at me last Tuesday, all countin' and measurin'. I know dat look. My mama had dat look on her de day dey took her from us, sold her down de river and we ain't never heard from her no more. Not one word. Like she just... gone into de earth.

I ain't goin' that way, John. I ain't.

Dere's a path, John — old Solomon told me of it, follow de drinkin' gourd in de sky, keep de North Star on your right shoulder till you cross where dat river bend hard. Dere's folks waitin' on de other side what help colored folk get free — I heard it whispered at de well, heard it in de hymns we ain't supposed to understand de real meanin' of. "Wade in de water" — dat ain't just about baptizin', John. Dat's about crossin' over. Dat's about *freedom*.

I want you to come wit me.

I know it's a hard road. I know dey got dogs, and dey got men wit guns, and de swamp got things dat bite worse than any overseer whip. But John — what we got here? What we got but wakin' up not knowin' if today de day dey tear us apart forever? I rather die free in a ditch somewhere up North dan live one more day not knowin' if I'm gon' see your face come sundown.

*[softer now, reaching for something wrapped in cloth]*

Look here. Look what I done made for you. Took me three weeks, hidin' de needle, workin' by firelight when everybody sleep. Dese ain't work clothes, John. Dese ain't clothes for pickin' or plowin' or bendin' your back for no master's profit.

Dese is *free* clothes.

I sewed 'em thinkin' 'bout you walkin' down a street somewhere up North, head high, nobody callin' you "boy," nobody ownin' your shadow. I sewed hope right into dese stitches, John. Every one of 'em.

Take dem. Wear dem when we cross dat river. Let dem be de first thing dat touch your skin as a free man.

We goin' together, John. Under dat North Star. Ain't nobody sellin' us apart — not while I got breath in my body and legs dat can run.

You wit me?
